name: Wei Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Wei. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm learning to run the winder at the Grayson shaft, the zinc mine north of town. The winder is the big engine that raises and lowers the cage, the lift that takes the men a kilometre and a half down, and the skips that bring the ore up. Most of it runs on automatic now, but the safety rules still say a qualified person sits in the chair when people are in the cage. I'm not qualified yet; I sit next to Gareth, who's been doing it for thirty years, and I take over when he lets me. It's calm work, but you never forget there are forty men hanging on that rope.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the winder?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I had the family hardware shop on Mill Street for twenty-five years, my father's before me. A big warehouse store opened by the highway and that was that. I closed it myself, paid every supplier, and I didn't ask anybody for a handout. That took our savings, so now we've maybe three weeks in the bank. The mine took me on at fifty-five, and my son-in-law, who's an electrician there, put a word in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, people always get carried away with the next big thing. At church coffee I'd say it's good, honest work that matters, not gadgets. I don't post things online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I finish my training, get my certificate and work until the pension. I lost the shop to a cheaper competitor once, so I don't mind if the robots stay in the brochure for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and aim to pass the winder exam within the year. I'd keep using that AI program my son-in-law put on the computer to go over the rule book, now and then. And we'd start putting a little aside again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Comfortable, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI to study the rule book. How does that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, once I got used to it. I type in a rule I don't understand and it explains it like a patient teacher. Gareth laughs at me for it, but he's also asked me to look something up for him twice. I wouldn't let it run the winder, mind you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would passing the winder exam change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean a proper wage, about a fifth more, and some respect. I'd stop being 'the shopkeeper' to the young ones. Lucia would like that too; she says I've been quiet since the shop.

S0.say: He'd say at church coffee that people always get carried away with the next big thing and that honest work matters more than gadgets.
S0.think: He thinks it means he can finish his training, get certified and work until his pension, and he's glad robots would stay in the brochure for a while.
S0.do: Keeps working and aims to pass the winder exam within a year, using AI now and then to study the rule book. Starts saving a little again.
S0.quote: I lost the shop to a cheaper competitor once, so I don't mind if the robots stay in the brochure for a while.
S0.fieldNote: Wei carries quiet pride in closing his shop honestly without help, and that shapes how he talks about work. He's a cautious but real AI user, impressed enough that even his old-school mentor now asks for lookups. Passing the exam is about respect as much as money.

steps.text: Pass the Grayson winder exam within the year
Go over the winder rule book with the AI program now and then
Start putting a little aside again

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market will decide, and people have to work hard and adapt like we always have. I'd say young men should get an apprenticeship in something that'll last. At church I'd say look after your families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think winders are already half automatic, so the question is when the rules change. The only thing between me and a computer is a line in the safety rules, and lines in rule books can be rubbed out. But rules on hoisting people move slowly, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the certificate as fast as I could, because a qualified winderman is the last to go. I'd put fifty a week aside for a rainy day. And I'd watch what the other mines do, and if they move to full automatic, I'd learn whatever system they bring in, once I see it working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think rules on hoisting people move slowly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if a cage drops, everybody is on the news. Nobody in an office wants to sign the paper that says a computer alone can carry forty men. I could be wrong; I'm a shopkeeper, not a lawyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be thinking about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth, funnily enough. He's sixty-one, best winderman I've ever seen, and he doesn't want anything to do with computers. If they go automatic, he'd retire, and I'd lose my teacher before I'm finished.

S1.say: He'd say the market will decide and people must work hard and adapt as always, advising young men to get apprenticeships that last.
S1.think: He thinks only a line in the safety rules stands between him and a computer, though he suspects rules on hoisting people change slowly.
S1.do: Hurries to finish his winder certificate and saves fifty a week. Watches other mines and learns any new automatic system once he sees it working.
S1.quote: The only thing between me and a computer is a line in the safety rules, and lines in rule books can be rubbed out.
S1.fieldNote: Wei has a sharp sense of where his job's protection comes from: a single safety rule. He's honest that he isn't sure how slowly rules will change. His steady, 'once it's proven' attitude to technology shows in his plan to watch other mines first.

steps.text: Finish the winder certificate as fast as he can
Put fifty a week aside for a rainy day
Learn any automatic winder system once he's seen it working elsewhere

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking work in 2028. Well. Sitting in the winder chair is thinking work, if you're honest about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At church coffee I'd say the rules on carrying men down a shaft won't change overnight, whatever the computers can do. I'd say a sensible company keeps a person in the chair. And I'd say young men should learn a trade with their hands, because that's got a few more years in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the winder already runs itself, and what I do in the chair is watch and decide when to stop it. That's exactly the work a thinking computer could do in 2028. The only thing in the way is the rule book, and if the machine really is as good as a person, somebody in an office will sign the paper sooner than I'd like. I'd be sixty, five years short of my pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still pass the certificate this year, because a qualified man is the last to go. But I'd also ask the shaft foreman if I could join the crew that inspects the rope and greases the sheaves, because that's hands-on work that lasts till 2031. We'd cut everything extra and put about fifty a week aside. And I'd do weekend repair jobs with my son-in-law, taps and fences and door hinges, the things I used to sell parts for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd keep it in my chest. Like the day the warehouse store opened and I still had a full shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Gareth do if the chair went to a computer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth would retire that day, he's sixty-one and he's said so. He'd shake my hand and tell me the rope crew is honest work. And he'd be right, but I'd miss the chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still pass the certificate. Why, if the chair might go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't know when the rule book changes, and nobody else does either. If the rule book holds till 2031, the certificate is my wage. If it doesn't, at least I've finished something, which matters to me after the shop.

S2.say: The rules on carrying men down a shaft won't change overnight, whatever the computers can do. Young men should learn a trade with their hands, because that's got a few more years in it.
S2.think: What I do in the winder chair is watch and decide when to stop, which is exactly the work a thinking computer could do in 2028. Only the rule book stands in the way, and I'd be sixty, five years short of my pension.
S2.do: Passes the winder certificate this year anyway, and asks to join the rope inspection crew, hands-on work that lasts until 2031. Cuts extras to save about fifty a week and does weekend repair jobs with his son-in-law.
S2.feel: Anxious but keeping it in his chest, like the day the warehouse store opened while his shop was still full.
S2.quote: Sitting in the winder chair is thinking work, if you're honest about it.
S2.fieldNote: Wei made a sharp point: his job looks like machine work but is really watching and deciding, which is the thinking work that goes first. His defence is the safety rule book plus a fallback to hands-on rope work until 2031. He still wants to finish his certificate, because finishing things matters to him after losing the shop.

steps.text: Ask to join the Grayson rope inspection crew, which lasts until 2031
Cut extras and save about fifty a week
Do weekend repair jobs around town with his son-in-law

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031 for the thinking. I'd be sixty-three. Pension at sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people have time to prepare, and they should get on with it instead of complaining. At church I'd say look after your families and learn something solid. That's what I'd tell anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd make it. The chair could go in 2031, but the rule book always lags a few years, and the rope crew lasts till 2034. If the rule book buys me two years and my son-in-law's toolbox buys me one more, I'm there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the certificate this year and work every shift I can, saving about sixty a week. I'd do weekend repair jobs with my son-in-law. And I'd keep using the AI to study, a bit more than now, because by 2031 I'd want to understand what's replacing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's a manageable worry. I can count the years on one hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why learn about the thing that's replacing you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if they keep one man to watch the computer, I want it to be me. And my father taught me it’s better to understand a new tool than to be afraid of it. He said that about every tool in the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lucia say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucia would say stop counting and go to sleep. Then she'd count with me. She's better at it than I am.

S3.say: People have time to prepare, and they should get on with it instead of complaining. Look after your families and learn something solid.
S3.think: I think I'd make it: the chair could go in 2031, but the rule book lags and the rope crew lasts till 2034. If the rule book buys me two years and my son-in-law's toolbox buys me one more, I'm there.
S3.do: Gets his winder certificate this year and works every shift he can, saving about sixty a week. Does weekend repair jobs with his son-in-law and studies with the AI more often to understand the system replacing him.
S3.feel: Uneasy but manageable, with the years countable on one hand.
S3.quote: My father taught me it’s better to understand a new tool than to be afraid of it.
S3.fieldNote: Wei builds a layered plan to reach his pension: the certificate, the slow rule book, then weekend work. His steady approach shows in studying the system that may replace him so he could be the one kept to watch it. His wife is his quiet partner in the arithmetic.

steps.text: Get the winder certificate and save about sixty a week
Do weekend repair jobs with his son-in-law
Study the automatic winder system with the AI more often

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. I'd be sixty-eight. Retired three years by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for everybody to get ready, and young people should take apprenticeships now. I'd say it at church coffee. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd finish my certificate, work the chair to sixty-five and hand it on. By 2036 the winder can run itself, and I'll be teaching my grandson to fix a dripping tap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, finish the winder certificate and save a little each month. When a new system comes in, I'd learn it with everyone else. No big moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit sad for Gareth's kind of work, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why sad for Gareth's kind of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a winderman is trusted with forty lives, and that trust goes to a computer. I'm not against it if it's safer. I'm just sorry nobody will be proud of that job any more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the shop still be on your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Always a little. I'd like to finish at the mine owing nobody, the way I closed the shop. With ten years, I think I can.

S4.say: There’s time for everybody to get ready, and nobody needs to do anything dramatic. Young people should take apprenticeships now.
S4.think: I'd be fine: finish my certificate, work the chair to sixty-five and hand it on. By 2036 the winder can run itself, and I'll be teaching my grandson to fix a dripping tap.
S4.do: Keeps working, finishes the winder certificate and saves a little each month. Learns any new system when it comes in, alongside everyone else, with no big moves.
S4.feel: Calm, with some sadness for the old pride of the winderman's job.
S4.quote: By 2036 the winder can run itself, and I'll be teaching my grandson to fix a dripping tap.
S4.fieldNote: With the long timeline Wei retires before anything changes and is calm. What he mourns is the trust and pride of the winderman's job, not the wage. Finishing debt-free remains his measure of a good working life.

steps.text: Finish the winder certificate and work the chair to sixty-five
Save a little each month until retiring

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because a thinking computer could take the winder chair in 2028, and I'd be five years short of the pension with nothing in the bank. What would help is the company keeping people like me on to the pension in some job, even sweeping, and proper apprenticeships for the young ones. I don't want a cheque for nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people are proud of. I closed my shop owing nobody a penny. I'd like to finish at the mine the same way, owing nobody and on my own two feet. That matters to men like me.

headlineQuote: I closed my shop owing nobody a penny. I'd like to finish at the mine the same way, owing nobody and on my own two feet.
portrait: Wei Rossi is 58 and is training to run the winder, the engine that raises and lowers the cage, at the Grayson zinc mine, after closing his family hardware shop when a warehouse store opened. He paid every supplier without help, which left about three weeks of savings, and he is proud of it. He uses AI now and then to study the rule book and believes the safety rules on hoisting people are what keep a person in the chair. He is calm in a plateau and uneasy in steady disruption. AGI by 2028 makes him anxious because he sees that watching the winder is thinking work that could go first, so he'd fall back on hands-on rope work and weekend repairs. With five or ten years he expects to reach his pension, sad only for the lost pride of the winderman's job.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because a thinking computer could take the winder chair when he's five years short of the pension with almost nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: The company keeping older workers on until their pension in some job, even sweeping, and proper apprenticeships for young people rather than cheques for nothing.
